finding.claim: Mass assignment / privilege escalation: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it, so a user can overwrite any field such as role, isAdmin, id, email or permissions. The response also returns the full req.user object, which could leak internal fields.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body of an authenticated PUT /me request (req.body)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists arbitrary attacker-chosen attributes on the user record

trace.note: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) merges all body keys with no allowlist
req.store.save(req.user) persists the modified user, including any escalated fields
res.json(req.user) returns the whole user object

finding.guards_checked: Looked for a field allowlist, schema validation or role-field denylist in users.js and found none. The sibling route /me/profile at lines 10-12 destructures only displayName and bio, so the safe pattern exists but is not applied here. The authentication middleware that sets req.user is not in this repository, so it could not be checked. users.js is the only source file. An authenticated low-privilege user is enough to exploit this.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, users.js:6 persists it and users.js:7 returns the whole user, while the safe sibling at users.js:11-12 destructures only displayName and bio; the auth middleware is not in the repo, but any authenticated user can reach it and would gain the ability to set role/admin fields (the exact field names depend on the user model, which isn't visible).
